articles.summary: Wall Street doubts gold’s near-term strength, Main Street maintains bullish minority as central banks take center stage  KitcoGold set for steep weekly loss as rising oil prices bolster Fed rate hike bets  ReutersUBS sees dip buyers stepping in to support gold at this level  Investing.com IndiaGold Slides Below $4,000  TradingViewGold prices fall 26% from peak: Should buyers expect further correction or a rebound?  Moneycontrol.com
articles.full_text:
(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline as rising oil prices, persistent inflation fears, and expectations for further Federal Reserve tightening overwhelmed safe-haven demand, while Thursday's technology-led equity selloff triggered another wave of liquidations that pushed the precious metal back below $4,000 per ounce.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $4,164.69 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal managed to eke out some early gains as traders continued to assess renewed U.S.-Iran tensions and the inflationary impact of disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. But the rally quickly stalled, with gold setting its weekly high of $4,190.17 per ounce early Monday morning before sellers took control as rising energy prices and elevated Treasury yields reinforced expectations that the Fed would maintain their restrictive monetary policy.
The selling accelerated through Monday and Tuesday trading, with gold breaking below $4,150 as markets continued to digest the previous week's hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI reports. The yellow metal attempted to stabilize on Wednesday as Treasury yields eased, but the recovery proved short-lived as traders remained focused on the risk of another Fed rate hike before year-end.
Gold prices plunged Thursday as a sharp technology-led equity selloff triggered broader market liquidations, even as Treasury yields and the dollar weakened. Renewed concerns about the AI sector and speculation about possible intervention in the Japanese yen added to the uncertainty, while renewed Middle East tensions pushed oil prices higher. The selling carried over into Friday, with gold set its weekly low of $3,975.10 per ounce – its lowest level since early June – around an hour after the North American open, and prices oscillated on both sides of $4,000-per-ounce heading into the weekly close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street pessimism on the rise after gold’s steep slide, while Main Street saw more silver lining despite the yellow metal’s recent underperformance.
“Gold, basis spot, was sold to a new three-month low before the weekend, slightly below $3990,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “It recovered but the technical tone still looks weak. The momentum indicators are not rising and the five- and 20-day moving averages are falling. Initial resistance is seen in the 4065-4075 area.”
“Half of the G10 central banks meet next week and only the RBNZ is likely to hike,” Chandler added. “Still, the others, including the Fed, will keep the door open to hikes before the end of the year.”
“Unchanged,” said Adrian Day, president of Adrian Day Asset Management. “More back and forth, but still think $4,000 will hold, or maybe just a little below.”
“Up,” said James Stanley, senior market strategist at Forex.com. “The $4k test has held so far, and while it may take a bit for the tide to turn, I think the case is still strong for $4k support – unless something breaks in the US economy which could lead to a risk aversion run. But even in that backdrop, I’m biased towards longer-term accumulation.”
“Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “The sell-off in the stock market this week triggered margin calls. As always, investors seeking liquidity to meet those margin calls turned to THE most liquid asset on earth… gold. The selling pressure took gold back below $4,000 per ounce.”
“I do not expect gold to remain below $4,000 very long,” Checkan said. “Barring any surprises from next Wednesday’s interest rate announcement from the Federal Open Market Committee, I would expect gold to bounce off these lows as bargain hunters snatch up as much cheap gold as they are able.”
Kevin Grady, president of Phoenix Futures and Options, said gold continues to trade inversely to interest rates, but there’s also broader concerns impacting the yellow metal.
“We're all thinking about rates, and I know we're following daily yields and things like that,” he said. “But it's also the long-term picture that people are looking at and seeing that there is a crack in the bond market, and even historically, that rates are higher.”
It's hard to see, because you're not really getting a lot of color,” Grady said. “A lot of commercials have decreased their trading. You're not seeing the volumes that we've had in the past. I think it's one of those things where gold has been trying to see the next leg up, and we just haven't had it.”
Grady said that a number of longs came into the market as gold posted its recent gains, and they were waiting for a good exit, but it didn’t come, and now they have no choice but to exit at lower prices and into thin liquidity.
“When you look at daily volumes at 129,000 contracts, that's what we used to do in open outcry! Once the markets went electronic, we were doing over 400,000 easily,” he said. “I think what's happening now is that it's very thin, and when you see people start to get out, it's just exacerbated the moves.”
Grady said that between the Iran war’s renewed threats of escalation, Russia-Ukraine getting worse, the risk of a hawkish Fed next week, and the looming midterm elections, people are wary of putting their money into the markets – any markets.
“That move [on Thursday], I think scared a lot of people away from saying, ‘Hey, let me go in right before a big meeting or a big decision where I don't know where it's going to be, and let me take a position.’ Because getting out of that position can be deadly.”
“I think that move yesterday is going to put a lot of people on the sidelines.”
Turning to Wednesday’s Fed meeting, Grady said that even if markets are pricing in a hold, under current conditions, they really can’t be sure
“What is the Fed going to do? The market's saying, no, he's not going to raise rates, but maybe he tries to shock people,” he said. “I don't think he should, but you just don't know. There's just too much uncertainty. A lot of people, especially professional traders, are saying, ‘This isn't trading right now, it's guessing.’”
“I was speaking with a friend of mine yesterday who's a big trader on the floor with me, in gold, and we were talking about [this],” he said “It isn't just that you’re a trader and you're putting on positions. As a trader, you're a risk manager. And if you're not a good risk manager, you're not going to be a successful trader. I think right now, when you look at the upside or downside to putting on a trade, what are the odds of this trade working? Markets have gotten so thin… I just think the upside is not worth it.”
Grady said that if gold does see a break below $4,000, we’ll soon be approaching levels where prices held during earlier selloffs.
“But I will tell you, underneath those levels is going to be stops, and everyone knows that,” he said. “Being long in front of those… it's always nice to buy in front of the support level, but when it breaks that support level, it could be dangerous. So I think people have to really watch out.”
This week, 17 analysts participated in the Kitco News Gold Survey, with the largest portion of Wall Street sentiment sliding into the bearish camp after gold’s precipitous drop below $4,000. Four experts, or 24%, expect to see gold prices gain ground during the week ahead, while seven, representing 41%, see the yellow metal declining further. The remaining six analysts, 35% of the total, said they couldn’t predict gold’s direction, or expected sideways trading next week.
Meanwhile, 161 votes were cast in Kitco’s online poll, with Main Street investors considerably more bullish than their professional counterparts despite gold’s late-week slide. 67 retail traders, or 42%, looked for gold prices to rise next week, while 41 others, or 26%, predicted the yellow metal would lose more ground. The remaining 53 investors, representing 33% of the total, expected to see consolidation during the week ahead.
Central banks will dominate next week’s economic news, with rate decisions from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Canada and Japan, but markets will also have a raft of growth, consumer and housing data to digest.
The U.S. calendar kicks off Tuesday morning with Durable Goods Orders, Consumer Confidence, and New Home Sales.
Then on Wednesday morning, the Bank of Canada will issue its monetary policy decision, followed by the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decision in the afternoon.
Thursday morning will see the ECB’s monetary policy decision, along with Advance US Q3 GDP and PCE, and weekly jobless claims, with the Bank of Japan’s monetary policy decision coming overnight to cap the week’s key data.
Sean Lusk, co-director of commercial hedging at Walsh Trading, said the Iran conflict – and its impact on oil prices, inflation expectations, and Fed rate projections – continues to cap gold’s potential gains.
“It's just an impediment to any rally in gold,” he said. “Now, there could be an 11th hour deal over the weekend for a ceasefire, but I don't know… It looks like the market, at least the energy space, is really priced in that this thing is going to escalate in the near term. Big time.”
Lusk said he’s optimistic about productivity gains from AI, but the broader economy won’t do well for a while.
“Bond yields aren't coming off anytime soon, which means housing prices are still going to decline – obviously there's going to be winners and losers in that space – but if you do have declining home values, where the sellers far outpace buyers by a wide margin, I don't think gold in that context is still at $4,000 an ounce. articles.summary: October 2026 FOMC Meeting Preview: Will the Fed Raise Rates Again? What Does This Mean for US Stocks?  TradingKey

The upcoming Federal Reserve FOMC meeting focuses on potential rate adjustments amid persistent inflation and shifting labor markets, with markets largely anticipating a rate pause in October while pricing in future tightening risks. Rising interest rates elevate Treasury yields and borrowing costs, creating capital pressure for high-valuation tech and AI infrastructure firms like Oracle and CoreWeave, which rely heavily on substantial capital investments. Investors must monitor rate expectations, Treasury yields, and corporate cash flows to evaluate how financing costs and investment returns impact growth stock valuations and AI sector profitability.
TradingKey - The Federal Reserve will hold its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting from October 27 to 28, Eastern Time. Inflationary pressures and labor market shifts have heightened monetary policy uncertainty, with the market focusing on whether the Fed will raise interest rates again and how subsequent policy signals will affect US stocks.
As of October 22, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, the market estimated an approximately 90.6% probability that the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged in October, and an approximately 9.4% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike.
On September 16, the Fed raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. The key focus of this meeting lies in whether the Fed will continue to tighten policy and what signals it will release regarding the future rate path.
[Source: CME]
The market currently expects the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates unchanged in October, but inflationary pressures remain an important factor influencing subsequent policy. US CPI rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, higher than August's 3.4%; core CPI rose 2.6% year-on-year, also higher than the previous reading of 2.4%, showing that inflationary pressures have not yet fully eased.
Meanwhile, slowing job growth may limit room for the Federal Reserve to tighten policy further. The Fed needs to comprehensively evaluate inflation trends, the labor market, and economic growth to balance price stability and employment goals.
According to the September dot plot, Fed officials' median forecast for the federal funds rate at the end of 2026 and 2027 was 4.1%, higher than the June forecasts of 3.8% and 3.6%. This reflects a more hawkish stance among officials regarding the future rate path compared to before, but it does not mean the Fed has committed to continuing rate hikes.
[Source: Federalreserve]
Therefore, even if rate hikes are paused in October, the risk of subsequent rate increases has not disappeared. Investors should focus on the Fed's assessment of inflation and employment, as well as whether the post-meeting statement signals further policy tightening in December.
Rising interest rates may push up Treasury yields and corporate borrowing costs, putting pressure on high-valuation growth stocks. The construction of AI data centers and GPU procurement require substantial capital investments; as a result, financing costs, project commissioning timelines, and investment returns have become key market focuses.
Take Oracle (ORCL) and CoreWeave (CRWV) as examples. In the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, Oracle's capital expenditures were approximately $28.5 billion, and free cash flow stood at negative $5.4 billion, reflecting the capital demands driven by AI infrastructure expansion. During the same period, the company's operating cash flow was approximately $23.1 billion, demonstrating that it still possesses strong operating cash flow generation capabilities.
CoreWeave, meanwhile, relies more heavily on external financing to support its data center expansion. In the second quarter of 2026, its net interest expense was approximately $640 million, making financing costs and debt service pressures key areas of concern.
If interest rates remain high for an extended period, costs for new financing and debt refinancing for certain companies may rise. However, the ultimate impact will depend on debt maturities, fixed or floating rate arrangements, and credit spreads.
For AI infrastructure companies, investors should also focus on whether revenue growth can translate into profits and cash flow, as well as whether additional capital expenditures can yield reasonable returns.
If the Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady and signals that inflation is gradually easing, growth stock valuations could find support. However, if the Fed delivers a surprise rate hike or hints at potential policy tightening in December, Treasury yields and borrowing costs may rise further, putting greater pressure on high-valuation tech stocks and AI infrastructure companies with substantial financing needs.
Investors should focus on three key metrics: first, changes in rate futures pricing for the December meeting; second, U.S. Treasury yields and corporate credit spreads to gauge shifting interest rate expectations and financing risks; and third, the capital expenditures, free cash flow, and financing arrangements of companies like Oracle and CoreWeave to assess whether AI investments can translate into actual returns.
Overall, the key to the October meeting lies not only in whether a rate hike occurs, but also in how the Federal Reserve shapes future rate expectations. For AI-related stocks, the interest rate environment must be evaluated alongside corporate earnings, cash flows, and returns on investment, making it difficult to determine future stock price trends based on a single rate decision alone.

articles.title: KOSPI rebounds after Solidigm IPO suspension… FOMC and earnings in focus - 머니투데이
articles.summary: KOSPI rebounds after Solidigm IPO suspension… FOMC and earnings in focus  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
The KOSPI index fell by 2% after experiencing sharp fluctuations last week amid controversies over the profitability of artificial intelligence (AI) investments and the re-escalation of armed conflict in the Middle East. This week, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting and Israel's general election are scheduled, followed by the third-quarter earnings releases from SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Interest rates, international oil prices, and semiconductor performance are expected to determine the direction of the stock market.
According to Korea Exchange on the 25th, the KOSPI index closed at 5550.30 on the 23rd, down 117.75 points (2.08%) from Jeonju. Gains and losses alternated over the five-day period, and a buy-side sidecar (futures market circuit breaker) was triggered in the KOSPI market on the 21st. Retail investors and foreign investors made net sales of 1.1021 trillion won and 719.9 billion won, respectively, while institutional investors made net purchases of 419 billion won. Foreign investors made net sales of SK Hynix worth 863.7 billion won, while making net purchases of Samsung Electronics worth 783.8 billion won.
The burden of AI investment by major U.S. tech companies fueled stock market volatility last week. Meta's third-quarter revenue increased by 26% year-on-year, but its free cash flow (FCF—the amount of cash generated from operating activities minus capital expenditures) turned into a deficit of $2.12 billion due to large-scale capital investments. Concerns grew over whether AI capital investment could continue to expand amid high oil prices and rising market interest rates, causing the NASDAQ index to fall by 2.60% on the 22nd (local time). This was the largest drop since June this year.
On the 23rd, domestic semiconductor stocks rebounded after SK Hynix announced it would suspend its consideration of a U.S. NASDAQ listing for its grandchild company, Solidigm. As concerns over shareholder value dilution from the grandchild company's listing eased, SK Hynix closed at 1,277,000 won, up 4.42% from the previous day. Samsung Electronics also ended trading at 215,500 won, up 0.47%. On that day, the KOSPI closed with a 0.3% gain.
Events that could impact the domestic stock market are also scheduled for this week. The Federal Reserve System (Federal Reserve) will hold its FOMC meeting on the 27th and 28th (local time). According to analysis by NH Investment & Securities, the probability of an interest rate freeze at this meeting, as reflected in the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) FedWatch, is 85.6%. The market is paying close attention not just to the interest rate decision itself, but to how much the Federal Reserve will leave open the possibility of additional rate hikes after December.
SK Hynix will release its third-quarter earnings on the 28th, and Samsung Electronics will announce its finalized third-quarter results on the 29th. At the earnings briefing, market attention is focused on whether plans for future AI semiconductor demand and capital investment, as well as additional shareholder return measures such as share buybacks, will be disclosed.
Stock prices have undergone significant corrections, resulting in a state of low price burden, according to analysis. Kim Dong-won, head of the Research Division at KB Securities, stated, "The KOSPI appears to have passed through the peak of concerns after forming two lows on July 29 (5262) and October 15 (5450), confirming a W-shaped bottom." He added, "The valuations of the KOSPI, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix have entered a historically undervalued range below levels seen during past financial crises. Additionally, U.S. 10-year Treasury yields appear to have formed a short-term peak in the mid-5% range, suggesting that the pace and slope of future interest rate increases are likely to be gradual."
However, it is noted as a burden that large volumes of selling from investors who bought at high prices during the rebound could be released, given that the index has fallen significantly from its peak. The current level of the KOSPI index is down 40.86% from the all-time high (9385.59) recorded intraday in June last month.
The Middle East situation could also increase stock market volatility. Na Jeong-hwan, a researcher at NH Investment & Securities, commented on Israel's general election on the 27th (local time) and the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 (local time), stating, "Both elections are major political events that will influence the direction of the Iran war and the continuation of military operations." He added, "In particular, whether the U.S. and Israel expand their military operations against Iran after the elections is expected to act as a key variable for international oil prices and Middle East geopolitical risks."

President Donald Trump has intensified criticism of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy after its September rate increase, raising concerns about borrowing costs and the outlook for U.S. stocks. The dispute centers on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the central bank's efforts to contain inflation, with potential consequences for major indexes and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage point in September, bringing the target range to 3.75%-4.00%. According to The Motley Fool, persistent inflation could prompt additional increases, while higher financing costs could slow AI data center construction, a major driver of equity market gains.
Market pricing tracked by CME Group's FedWatch Tool indicated a 64% probability of at least another 0.75 percentage point in rate increases by September 2027. The Federal Open Market Committee was scheduled to meet on October 27-28, 2026, as investors assessed the inflation outlook and the possibility of further monetary tightening.
In an interview with Time, Trump directed his criticism primarily at the Federal Reserve's board, while distinguishing Warsh from other policymakers.
"The problem is that the Fed board is very hostile" Trump said in the interview, according to the account published by Bloomberg-related news coverage.
Trump also said he did not personally blame Warsh for the board's decision and suggested the chair faced opposition within the committee.
"It's a problem because we have a very hostile Fed board," Trump said.
He added that he disagreed with the September decision and believed the board's position was contributing to tensions over monetary policy.
"I don't blame Kevin Warsh. I probably would have voted against the board if I were him," Trump said.
Trump had also expressed confidence in Warsh while arguing that the chair faced a difficult position within the committee. Speaking to reporters on September 16, the day of the rate increase, he criticized the level of borrowing costs and the board's approach.
"I'm relying on Kevin, but he's got a very tough board," Trump said.
He argued that interest rates remained too high and accused policymakers of making decisions that could harm his administration's economic performance.
"The interest rates are too high; they're not appropriate.... The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing," Trump said.
Trump also alleged that the board's decisions were politically motivated, although the source material did not establish evidence supporting that accusation.
"raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do," Trump said.
Inflation remains a central factor behind the Fed's decisions. According to the source reports, U.S. consumer inflation reached 4.2% in May 2026, a three-year high, and stood at 3.7% year over year in September. Both readings exceeded the Federal Reserve's long-term inflation target of 2%.
Economic pressures include tariffs introduced by the Trump administration and energy supply disruptions associated with the war involving Iran. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimated that tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to goods-price inflation by February 2026.
The conflict involving Iran has also disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to higher fuel costs. The source report said the disruption had affected a significant share of global petroleum flows and that restoring regional production and rebuilding inventories could take months.
Bond markets have reflected concerns about financing costs. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield reached 5.34% on October 1, 2026, its highest level in 24 years, according to the source report. Long-term yields influence corporate borrowing expenses and financing for capital-intensive projects such as AI data centers.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite have recorded substantial gains during Trump's presidency. However, The Motley Fool warned that renewed tension between the White House and the Federal Reserve, combined with further rate increases, could put downward pressure on equities if higher financing costs weaken investment.

articles.summary: Evercore Outlines Key Credit and Treasury Yield Thresholds That Could Signal AI Stock Market Correction  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
Evercore strategists have identified a series of financial market indicators that could signal a correction in artificial intelligence-related stocks following last week's technology sector selloff.
In a research note published on Sunday, a team led by Julian Emanuel said the recent declines marked the beginning of a price discovery phase for AI investments, with investors reassessing valuations, borrowing costs and the financial requirements of large-scale infrastructure development.
The firm identified four indicators that could signal a transition from the current bull market into a correction, or potentially a bear market if economic conditions deteriorate into recession.
Despite the identified risks, Evercore reiterated its year-end 2026 target of 7,750 for the S&P 500.
Credit Spreads and Earnings Revisions Among Key Indicators
Evercore highlighted four market developments that it believes warrant close attention as investors evaluate the sustainability of the AI-related equity rally.
The first is an increase in investment-grade credit default swap (CDS) spreads above their March peak of 68.33.
The second is a rise in high-yield CDS spreads beyond their previous high of 411.04.
CDS spreads reflect the cost of obtaining protection against a borrower's default. An increase generally indicates that market participants are demanding greater compensation for credit risk.
The third indicator is a reversal in the upward trend of analysts' earnings-per-share estimates, which could suggest that expectations for corporate profitability are weakening.
The fourth is a rise in the yield on 10-year US Treasury securities above 5.62%.
According to Evercore, these indicators could help determine whether recent market weakness remains concentrated in technology stocks or develops into a broader reassessment of financial asset valuations.
US Treasury Yield of 5.62% Identified as Fiscal Warning Level
Evercore's Washington policy team said a 10-year Treasury yield above 5.62% could increase concerns about US fiscal conditions and government borrowing costs.
The strategists noted that the recent yield peak of 5.36% provided a reference point for assessing further increases.
They described 5.62% as "a reasonable level at which alarm bells would be expected to ring."
The team referred to such a development as a potential "fiscal alarm bell."
Higher government bond yields can influence borrowing costs across the economy, including corporate debt financing and household lending.
They can also affect equity valuations by increasing the discount rates applied to expected future earnings.

articles.full_text:
In early Asian trading on Friday, the GBP/USD pair hovered around 1.3400, extending its recent modest upward trend. The key dynamic at play is this: UK inflation has rebounded more sharply than expected, providing the Bank of England with a clear rationale for raising interest rates and making the pound one of the highest-yielding currencies in Europe. Meanwhile, on the U.S. side, the Fed's "no rush to hike" stance has dampened bullish momentum, yet the absence of evidence disproving a year-end tightening path continues to cap the pound's upside. Together, these factors have given the exchange rate a seesaw‑like character—easy to rally but hard to plunge, with any meaningful breakout requiring a catalyst.
From the pound's perspective, the broad-based acceleration in inflation data has been the primary driver of its recent strength.
Data released Wednesday by the UK Office for National Statistics showed that, propelled by sharp increases in gasoline and diesel prices, September's CPI rose 3.
5% year-on-year, while core CPI climbed to 2.
8%, both exceeding market expectations.
This indicates that the UK's inflation rebound is not confined to temporary energy‑related shocks but is spreading into core components—precisely the kind of broadening that central banks most closely monitor.
Bank of England policymaker Glyn's recent remarks earned a score of 7.
4 out of 10, matching his historical average, yet his tone was unmistakably hawkish: he emphasized that wage‑driven disinflation has stalled at levels inconsistent with the 2% target, argued that policy should proactively guard against second-round effects, and warned that such risks are "greater than previously thought.
" Despite forward‑looking indicators suggesting wage growth is approaching 3.
5%, Glyn maintains that the labor market remains tight and that slack may have already peaked.
This stance reinforces a policy bias toward keeping monetary tightening in place for an extended period, thereby capping near-term downside for the pound.
For the pound, this amounts to a combination of "data validation plus official endorsement": as long as wages and service‑sector prices do not decelerate sharply, the path of rate hikes is likely to remain supported, and the pound's yield‑spread advantage will persist.

Traders are pricing in roughly a 98% probability that the Bank of England will raise interest rates by 25 basis points to 4.0% next month, with most already factoring in a second 25-basis-point hike at its final meeting in December. If realized, this would mark the central bank's first rate increase since 2023 and make it one of the few G10 policymakers still pursuing meaningful monetary tightening. ING analysts note that the pound's recent strength against the euro is not solely driven by domestic political sentiment: "It appears the pound has been riding on the coattails of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's surging popularity. In reality, the EUR/GBP move reflects both the pound's independent appreciation and the euro's independent depreciation." The firm acknowledges that "earlier this year we doubted the pound's gains could be sustained," but adds that "heightened market confidence in the Bank of England's rate-hike cycle—anticipating 25-bps increases in February and November—has turned the pound into a high‑yield currency in Europe." This view carries direct implications for GBP/USD: when the pound simultaneously benefits from a yield‑rate advantage and attractive capital‑allocation dynamics, any pullback against the dollar is more likely to find support at relatively elevated levels.
However, the upside for the British pound remains constrained by multiple factors. On the one hand, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell refrained last week from signaling the timing or necessity of future rate hikes, and nearly all economists surveyed expect the Fed to skip a hike in October and wait until December. This combination of "uncertainty about direction and a delayed timeline" has helped sustain the dollar's yield‑rate advantage while preventing a risk‑off reversal triggered by overly hawkish signals. For GBP/USD, this creates an environment where "the pound has catalysts, but the dollar has a floor": with the year‑end tightening path still unchallenged, the pair finds support at the bottom; yet the lack of fresh hawkish impetus in the near term leaves any breakout lacking momentum. On the other hand, ING expects fiscal policy to have only limited impact on the market, noting that "next week's UK budget is unlikely to reverse the recent move below 0.8400 in EUR/GBP," and judging that the cross pair "remains under pressure in the 0.8360–0.8430 range." This suggests that the pound's strength is more pronounced against European currencies like the euro, while its relative performance versus the U.S. dollar remains anchored by U.S. interest rates—investors should avoid simply extrapolating the euro‑related strength to GBP/USD.
UK retail sales data will be released later today, providing direct evidence of whether inflation has genuinely passed through to the consumer end. Should retail sales weaken, it could undermine the credibility of the "inflation–wages–rate hikes" transmission chain, triggering short-term profit-taking in the pound. Next week's UK budget is seen by market participants as having limited impact, though any fiscal expansion exceeding expectations could still indirectly disrupt the pound's trajectory via gilt yields. For investors, this suggests that, pending the release of the data, a range‑bound approach remains more prudent than a directional one, with the odds of successfully chasing rallies or cutting losses sharply diminishing.

Evercore strategists have identified several credit market, bond yield and corporate earnings indicators that could signal a broader correction in artificial intelligence-related stocks following last week's technology sector selloff.
In a research note published on Sunday, a team led by Julian Emanuel said the recent declines marked the beginning of a period of price discovery for AI-related investments, as investors reassessed valuations, financing requirements and the sustainability of corporate spending.
The strategists outlined four market indicators that they believe could signal a transition from the current bull market into a correction, with the possibility of a more prolonged decline if accompanied by an economic recession.
Evercore nevertheless maintained its year-end 2026 target of 7,750 for the S&P 500.
Evercore Highlights Four Market Risk Indicators
Evercore identified four developments that could indicate increasing pressure on the broader equity market and AI-related investments.
The first involves investment-grade credit default swap (CDS) spreads exceeding their March peak of 68.33.
The second concerns high-yield CDS spreads rising above their previous high of 411.04.
Credit default swaps are financial contracts used to provide protection against borrower defaults. Rising spreads generally indicate that investors are demanding higher compensation for credit risk.
The third indicator is a reversal in the upward trend of analysts' earnings-per-share revisions, which could suggest deteriorating expectations for corporate profitability.
The fourth is an increase in the yield on 10-year US Treasury securities above 5.62%.
According to Evercore, a combination of worsening credit conditions, weaker earnings expectations and higher government borrowing costs could place additional pressure on equity valuations.
Treasury Yield Above 5.62% Could Raise Fiscal Concerns
Evercore's Washington policy team identified a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.62% as a level that could prompt greater market attention to US fiscal conditions.
The team referred to the recent yield peak of 5.36% and described 5.62% as "a reasonable level at which alarm bells would be expected to ring."
The strategists characterised such a development as a potential "fiscal alarm bell."
Higher Treasury yields can increase borrowing costs for businesses and households while influencing the discount rates used to value future corporate earnings.
For technology companies whose valuations depend partly on expectations of long-term growth, sustained increases in bond yields can affect the present value assigned to anticipated profits.

articles.title: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week - Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.summary: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week  Bozeman Daily Chronicle
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A key update on inflation and its impact on consumer confidence, economic growth and interest rate policy will fill a busy calendar this week along with more big earnings reports.
They all arrive just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections that will determine the future makeup of Congress as the U.S. economy grapples with constantly shifting global trade conflicts and a global oil shortage brought on by the U.S. war with Iran. Inflation is stubbornly high, consumers are losing confidence and the resilient jobs market is showing more signs of stress.
Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead.
Consumer confidence keeps falling as inflation squeezes household budgets
Americans are losing confidence in the economy as rising prices for everything from gas to groceries guts budgets. The latest consumer confidence survey from business group The Conference Board on Tuesday is expected to show that consumer confidence kept shrinking in October.
The last report showed that confidence plunged in September to the lowest level in more than a decade. The October report is expected to show confidence kept weakening. Consumer confidence is down sharply from two years ago, according to the survey. In that time, the U.S. has waged a wide-ranging trade war with much of the world, including its neighbors and closest trading partners. The uncertainty around the sudden shifts in tariffs left businesses and consumers wary about planning ahead over worries about higher costs. The U.S. war with Iran that started in 2026 slashed global oil supplies and added more fuel to rising prices.
The Federal Reserve struggles to contain rising inflation
The Federal Reserve will close out a two-day meeting on Wednesday and is expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady following a hike at its September meeting. The central bank has been signaling that it is still worried about inflation and that it may have to continue raising rates to help tame rising costs. Wall Street still expects that one more rate hike is coming at the Fed's meeting in December.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more costly, which in turn can slow economic growth and cool stubbornly hot inflation. The Fed has to balance taming inflation with supporting the jobs market. Higher interest rates and slower economic growth could dampen rising inflation, but they could also hurt job growth at a time when the somewhat resilient employment market is showing signs of stress.
Economic growth faces the impact of stubborn inflation, weakening consumer confidence
The U.S. Department of Commerce on Thursday will release its initial report on economic growth during the third quarter and economists expect a sluggish result. Economists are forecasting that gross domestic product, which is the nation's output of goods and services, rose 1.7% from July through September. It's the first of three reports for third-quarter GDP and can be revised higher or lower.
The forecast for the initial assessment marks an easing from 2.2% growth during the second quarter. GDP growth has been slowing since the first quarter under pressure from higher oil prices fueling already stubbornly high inflation. Growth has been bolstered by a strong stock market and businesses investing in artificial intelligence technology. Households, though, have been struggling with higher costs on everything from gas to groceries eating up more of their budgets at the same time that average wages for workers stagnate.
Inflation keeps heating up as US war with Iran squeezes global oil supplies
The latest inflation update is expected to show that prices on everything from gasoline to clothing and groceries marched higher at a faster rate in September. The U.S. will release the personal consumption expenditures report, or PCE, on Thursday and economists expect that inflation jumped at a 3.7% rate, up from a 3.4% rate in August.
The PCE is the preferred measure of inflation used by the Fed, which wants to bring inflation down to its target rate of 2%. Several other measures of inflation have also moved stubbornly above a 3%. Inflation has been rising at an even sharper rate since the U.S. war with Iran started in February, essentially shutting down the vital Strait of Hormuz and stifling the global oil supply. That has prompted a surge in gasoline prices that have been a direct hit to household budgets. Higher diesel fuel costs raised the cost of shipping and warehousing goods, which businesses typically pass along to consumers.
The latest updates on retail sales show that household spending remains strong, on the surface. Much of that spending, though, is the result of paying higher costs, especially for gasoline.
Corporate earnings reports could shed light on AI investments and household spending
Investors have another busy week of earnings ahead, with reports from big names that could provide more insight on plans for AI spending and how inflation is influencing profits.
The most closely-watched reports this week are likely to be the big technology or technology-related companies that have seen their stock values surge as they heavily invest in artificial-intelligence technology with hopes for a big benefit. Google's parent company Alphabet reports its results on Wednesday, with Intel and Amazon reporting their latest results on Thursday. Analysts expect all three companies to report profit gains as Wall Street tries to determine whether their big AI investments will translate into future growth and whether their outsized stock values are justified.
A wide range of other companies will report results this week, shedding more light on inflation's impact across industries. Shipping company UPS and beverage giant Coca-Cola report results on Tuesday. Starbucks reports its results on Thursday, while oil giants Exxon Mobil and Chevron report their results on Friday.

articles.title: USD/JPY Weekly Outlook: AI earnings could overshadow the Fed and BoJ - FOREX.com
articles.summary: USD/JPY Weekly Outlook: AI earnings could overshadow the Fed and BoJ  FOREX.com

- USD/JPY increasingly moves with US yields, Nasdaq and volatility
- US Treasury yields tumble as global tech stocks weaken
- Fed and BoJ decisions face competition from tech earnings
- Bulls defend 156.68, but momentum indicators favour downside.
A sharp midweek unwind in US Treasury yields, driven by deteriorating sentiment towards AI-related investment, was enough to knock USD/JPY out of its narrow trading range between the 50 and 200-day moving averages last week. However, a stabilisation in sentiment towards the back end of the week was enough to reverse part of those moves on Friday, delivering a bullish signal on the daily chart.
Despite interest rate decisions from the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan this week, along with a smattering of top-tier economic data, you could arguably make the case that earnings updates from AI-related companies, particularly the massive hyperscalers, may be just as influential on USD/JPY's performance in the weeks ahead. Of particular interest will be guidance on AI capital expenditure and commentary on expected payback periods, including when those enormous investments may begin delivering on the hype already priced into markets.
One trade increasingly driving everything
As we highlighted in a separate analysis piece last week, sentiment towards AI-related investments is becoming a core driver of broader market movements, with traders seemingly adopting it as a proxy for the US growth outlook, influencing Treasury yields and, to a lesser extent, the US dollar.
Source: LSEG
The relationship has become increasingly strong as we've moved through October, with the correlation between USD/JPY and US 10-year Treasury yields flirting with +0.97 over five sessions, with similar readings for Nasdaq 100 futures and an equally strong inverse relationship with VIX futures.
While you need to be careful when assessing five-session correlations, you can see those relationships have also been evident over 10 and 20-session windows. The message is that markets which were previously fixated on crude oil movements now seem to be taking their cues from AI sentiment, suggesting it will be a key focal point for traders in the week ahead.
AI jitters drive a sharp Treasury rally
The deterioration in sentiment towards AI-related investments has coincided with a sharp rollover in US Treasury yields, mirroring the weakness seen across technology stocks and indices globally.
Source: LSEG
Over the past fortnight, US two-year Treasury yields have fallen 10.9 basis points, compared with 21.4 basis points for five-year yields and 25.6 basis points for the 10-year. The declines in the latter two tenors rank among the largest 2% of comparable two-week moves over the past year, underlining just how significant the shift has been.
The greater declines further along the curve have also seen the spread between two and 10-year Treasury yields flatten by 14.7 basis points, consistent with markets reassessing the US nominal growth outlook as doubts surrounding the returns on AI investment weigh on global technology shares. While it's not the only influence on yields, it has been the most prominent factor seen of late.
Hawkish Fed pricing unwinds fast
The sharp decline in US Treasury yields has also been mirrored at the immediate front end of the US interest rate curve, with traders substantially scaling back the amount of rate hikes expected from the Fed over the coming year. According to our fed funds futures model, cumulative tightening priced by the end of next year has fallen from 100.9 basis points at the time of the September Fed meeting to just 66.1 basis points now, an unwind of 34.8 basis points.
Source: TradingView
For this week's Fed decision, just 3.1 basis points of tightening is priced, equivalent to roughly a 12% probability of a 25 basis point hike. It really comes across as a placeholder meeting more than anything else, with markets now of the view that the Fed is likely to hike at its subsequent meeting in December, although confidence in that view has waned along the way.
With no new economic forecasts released at this meeting, the focus will be on any changes to the accompanying statement, the voting split, particularly whether there are dissenters in favour of a hike, and commentary from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh during his subsequent press conference.
BOJ expected to hold, December hike favoured
Like the Fed, the Bank of Japan is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its meeting on Friday, with markets favouring another 25 basis point hike in December. However, the probability of that outcome has also edged lower over recent weeks.
Unlike the Fed, the BoJ will release updated economic and inflation projections in its quarterly Outlook Report, which could provide important clues about the path of interest rates moving forward. Any changes in the accompanying policy statement, the voting split and commentary from Governor Ueda during his press conference will be the main areas of interest for traders when assessing whether the BoJ is still on track to hike in December.
AI earnings could overshadow central bank decisions
As the accompanying calendar shows, there's a raft of major tech earnings due this week, including updates from some of the world's largest hyperscalers. Of particular interest will be guidance on AI capital expenditure and whether the enormous sums being committed to the technology can deliver the returns investors are expecting.
Source: TradingView
As we saw following Meta's earnings call last week, concerns are growing about the ability to continue funding the massive capex rollout, along with uncertainty over not only when returns on those investments will materialise, but whether they will materialise at all.
In the absence of a major surprise from either the Fed or BoJ, these earnings updates could arguably be the more important market events for USD/JPY this week, which really says something about how one-dimensional markets feel right now.
Economic data risks taking a back seat
There's also a smattering of important economic data due this week, although whether it will have much influence on USD/JPY is another question.
Source: TradingView
In Japan, the BoJ's underlying inflation measures for September and Tokyo CPI for October, on the surface, seem like incredibly important releases. However, when September's Tokyo CPI report came in hot, markets barely blinked an eyelid, raising questions about whether anything on the Japanese economic calendar will really move the dial this week.
You could arguably make the same case for the US calendar, where the advance estimate of Q3 GDP on Thursday, along with personal income and spending figures, look to be the highlights. Even the core PCE deflator, still the Fed's preferred inflation measure, has struggled to generate meaningful market volatility over recent years, suggesting economic data may once again take a back seat to broader market sentiment.
USD/JPY technicals
Source: TradingView
As you can see on the USD/JPY chart, the abrupt decline in US Treasury yields midweek broke the stalemate between the 50 and 200-day moving averages that we'd seen over the past two weeks, sending the pair down to anchoring support at 156.68 on Friday.
As we saw on several occasions in late September, bulls stepped in to defend the level, driving the pair back above it into the close and delivering a dragonfly doji. While it doesn't come after a particularly pronounced downtrend, the pattern, like those seen beforehand, suggests bulls are lying in wait beneath 156.68.
That makes 156.68 the immediate support level beneath where the pair now trades, followed by 156.05, where the decline stalled on Friday. Below that, a more pronounced support zone comes into view between 155.50 and 155.00. Given what we saw last week, it would likely require either a very dovish surprise from the Fed, a very hawkish surprise from the BoJ, or another sharp deterioration in AI sentiment to see those levels tested. If that occurs, 154.50 and 152.90 are the next downside levels of note.
Having managed to reclaim 156.68, the focal point overhead is now the 50-day moving average at 157.58, followed by the 200-day moving average and resistance at 159.00.
While Friday delivered a bullish signal, the oscillators continue to warn bulls against getting carried away. RSI (14) has flipped beneath the neutral 50 level, while MACD has staged a bearish crossover and is on the cusp of turning negative. That suggests momentum is shifting to the downside, although the signal is not yet definitive.

- The Fed and ECB are likely to hold rates steady in October, while keeping December hikes on the table.
- Persistent inflation and resilient growth support further monetary tightening.
- French bond market tensions could constrain the ECB’s room to raise rates.
- Lower energy prices and tighter financing conditions could reduce the need for additional hikes next year.
- Central bank guidance will shape bond yields, while French fiscal risks could weigh on the euro.
The Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are likely to leave interest rates unchanged at their October meetings. However, a pause would not necessarily mark the end of monetary tightening. Persistent inflation and resilient economic activity support the case for further increases in December, although tensions in the French government bond market could constrain the ECB.
Inflation remains too high
Price pressures on both sides of the Atlantic remain too strong for central banks to declare victory. In the US, annual PCE inflation stood at 3.4% in August, while the core measure reached 3.0%. In the euro area, headline inflation rose to 3.8%, with core inflation at 2.5%.
The risk that higher energy costs will feed through to other goods and services continues to complicate the return to target. Meanwhile, relatively resilient economic activity reduces the likelihood that weaker demand alone will quickly contain inflation.
The forecasts presented in the source material point to annualised US GDP growth of 3.5% in the third quarter and quarterly growth of 0.3% in the euro area. Such readings would give policymakers additional room to maintain a restrictive stance.
Inflation measures in the US and the eurozone
October favours caution
Despite these inflation risks, recent central bank communication suggests that caution will prevail in October. Following September’s rate increases, policymakers have reasons to assess their effects before taking further action. Geopolitical uncertainty and higher government bond yields also strengthen the case for a pause.
For the Federal Reserve, the proximity of the US midterm elections adds political sensitivity to the upcoming meeting. This could reinforce the appeal of waiting, although the inflation outlook remains the central consideration.
French debt tensions complicate the ECB’s decision
France presents an additional challenge for the ECB. The spread between French and German ten-year government bond yields has approached 175 basis points, reflecting concerns about public finances and the government’s ability to deliver fiscal consolidation.
Another rapid rate increase could raise borrowing costs further and intensify market tensions. A December hike therefore remains conditional on the French debt market avoiding a more serious deterioration.
December hikes remain the base case
A further 25 - basis - point increase by both central banks in December remains the base case. The outlook for additional tightening next year is less clear.
A normalisation of oil supplies from the Middle East could lower energy prices and gradually ease inflation. At the same time, elevated long - term bond yields are already tightening financing conditions, potentially reducing the need for further policy rate increases.
Guidance will shape the market response
Markets will focus on the guidance accompanying any October pause. A clear signal that December hikes remain on the table could limit declines in short-term bond yields.
For the euro, however, monetary policy expectations are only part of the picture. A further deterioration in French public finances could weigh on the currency even if the ECB maintains a hawkish message.
EUR/USD: Downtrend channel remains intact
There is no doubt that EUR/USD has been trading within a descending channel since February 2026. The latest upward correction ended around 1.1279, and the pair is now moving lower again. The pattern of lower highs and lower lows confirms that sellers remain in control.
The nearest support lies at 1.1115, last week’s low. A break below this level could pave the way towards the channel’s lower boundary, near 1.1000. Conversely, a recovery above 1.1279 could allow the correction to extend towards the 1.1340 area.

Brent was on track for a third consecutive weekly gain.
Aramco evacuates headquarters
The latest rally followed a sharp escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis. Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, ordered staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran, in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province, and to work from home.
Saudi civil aviation authorities said one person was killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in eastern Saudi Arabia. A drone aimed at an Aramco facility at Shaybah was intercepted.
Analysts said the attacks suggested the Houthis now have the ability to strike deeper into Saudi Arabia, beyond their earlier focus on the Red Sea and the kingdom's western ports. The Houthis have also pushed toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping chokepoint at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Iran tensions in focus
Investors were also watching rising tensions with Iran. Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy claimed it struck four vessels involved in what it called illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf, and said three more ships hit mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. Those claims could not be independently verified.
President Donald Trump accused Iran of "making up fake hits" to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month, according to media reports.
"Markets are increasingly worried about renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf," ING analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note.
"Reports suggest President Trump is considering fresh strikes on Iran," they wrote, adding that the United States was reportedly reinforcing its military presence in the region with a second aircraft carrier.
ING said renewed escalation would undercut hopes for a de-escalation after the U.S. midterms. The bank said its earlier forecast for Brent to average $80 a barrel in the fourth quarter was now unattainable and raised its outlook.
Libya supply loss
Supply disruptions outside the Gulf added to the upward pressure. Libya's National Oil Corporation said a pipeline carrying crude from the Hamada and Tahara fields to the Zawiya export terminal had been shut, cutting production at both fields.
Libya, a member of OPEC, has frequently faced supply disruptions due to political instability and local disputes.
Russia-Ukraine talks
Partially offsetting the supply concerns, Russia said it was ready to resume U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine next month. Western sanctions on Russian energy exports have helped push oil prices higher, and any progress toward a peace deal could eventually ease supply concerns.
Impact on markets
The surge in oil prices has rippled across financial markets. Higher energy costs have revived fears of inflation and raised expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve may need to keep interest rates higher for longer.
The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023, and investors are watching its policy meeting on Oct. 27-28 for further signals. Traders see a possible increase in December.
Higher oil prices also weighed on gold, which fell toward its lowest level in nearly three months, and contributed to a broader risk-off mood that hit technology stocks and cryptocurrencies.
Consumers feel the pinch
For consumers, higher crude prices typically translate into higher gasoline and diesel prices within weeks. U.S. crude above $100 a barrel is likely to put pressure on fuel prices just as the country heads into the midterm elections, making energy costs a politically sensitive issue.
Airlines, shipping companies and other energy-intensive industries also face rising costs, which could be passed on to customers.
What's next
Oil traders will remain focused on developments in the Middle East, particularly the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis and the risk of renewed U.S. or Israeli strikes on Iran.
Any disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil passes, could send prices sharply higher. On the other hand, signs of de-escalation or progress in Russia-Ukraine peace talks could ease supply concerns.
Investors will also watch U.S. inventory data and next week's Fed meeting for clues on demand and the economic outlook.

- INTERVIEW
Interview with Milano Finanza
Interview with Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, conducted by Roberto Sommella on 21 October 2026
24 October 2026
Mr Cipollone, you have just attended a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Italian Banking Association. Was the digital euro one of the topics discussed?
We mainly talked about tokenisation. On the subject of the digital euro, I provided an update on the status of the debates on the legislation in Brussels and on the progress of our internal preparations within the Eurosystem.
Since you joined the ECB, payments have become one of the main focus areas of your work. Why are they so important for Europe’s future?
Because payments constitute a strategic infrastructure for Europe and, as a central bank, ensuring the smooth functioning of payment systems falls within our mandate. Whenever we buy something online or pay for a coffee, we think about the price of what we’re buying. But we hardly ever think about how the payment is made. Yet if the payment system stops working, the economy stops working.
Will the introduction of the digital euro help with this?
Yes. Today we can use money issued by the central bank only in the form of cash. But a growing share of our economic life takes place online, where banknotes can’t be used. The digital euro fills this gap. It gives people the freedom to make payments using an instrument that is equivalent to cash in terms of its nature and characteristics, such as privacy and covering all payment needs, but which also works where cash can’t be used.
Why has this now become necessary?
Ever more purchases are being made online. In Italy, for example, according to the latest available data, online payments grew from 6% of the total in 2019 to 24% in 2024. And I expect they’ve grown even more since then.
These online purchases are normally made via card payments and two thirds of these payments are made using non-European card schemes. For most euro area countries, this dependence on non-European operators is not limited to online payments but also extends to physical shops, because they don’t even have anything like Italy’s Bancomat that would enable payments to be made in local shops.
In short, for an essential service like payments, we are heavily dependent on an infrastructure over which we have no direct control.
So can the digital euro be described as a European digital sovereignty project?
The Eurosystem focuses on matters that are closely related to its mandate. And, as I said at the start, the smooth functioning of payment systems is one of our responsibilities. If we are critically dependent on third parties, it’s not easy to ensure this smooth functioning. In recent years Europe has learned that, for some essential services, we cannot rely only on third parties. We saw this with energy and we’re seeing it today with defence. And the same is true for payments.
The digital euro will give Europe an alternative of its own, bringing to the digital world what cash has always ensured: a secure form of public money that protects privacy and is accepted throughout the euro area.
Sovereignty doesn’t mean shutting third parties out. It means having the power to choose and knowing that, for an essential service like payments, Europe can also rely on its own strength.
Does this dependency bring any specific consequences for merchants too?
Yes, particularly for small merchants. Today the fees that a small shop pays can be up to four times higher than those paid by large operators. The digital euro will introduce a European alternative that will increase competition and, thanks to the caps on costs laid down by law, will help to reduce fees for those with less bargaining power.
From this perspective, it seems that there’s no time to waste.
Absolutely. In 2027 we will already launch a pilot based on real transactions carried out by the staff of the ECB and the other national central banks. It will serve to test the technology in real conditions and to build the digital euro hand-in-hand with the market.
36 market operators, of which seven are Italian, are already collaborating in the preparatory works. And we are now calling for e-commerce and mobile commerce operators to take part.
If the regulation is approved this year, the digital euro could be rolled out as early as 2029. When will the final decision be taken?
The decision can only be taken once the legislative negotiations that are under way in Brussels have been concluded. We hope that the regulation will be adopted by the end of the year, enabling the ECB’s Governing Council to issue a formal decision on issuance.
The adoption of the regulation will make it possible to complete the rulebook with the technical rules necessary for the market to prepare ahead of time. The ECB can get the infrastructure ready, but banks, payment system operators and merchants will also need time to adapt their systems and processes.
Will there be a limit on holdings of digital euro?
Yes, but there won’t be limits on payments. The limit applies to how much digital euro I can hold in a digital wallet, not how much I can spend. If a payment exceeds the available balance – when buying a car, for example – it will be possible to take the remainder automatically from the linked current account.
The limit on the amount of digital euro that can be held will safeguard financial stability, particularly in crisis situations. Our analyses show that with a properly calibrated limit, there will be no negative effects on the banking system.
Is it true that it will also work offline?
Yes. It will be possible to make payments in shops during a power cut or in remote and isolated areas where there’s no internet connection or where the connection is weak and sporadic. It will suffice to bring two devices together, as when using a contactless card today. The payment will be made directly between the payor and payee, without going via the internet. It means merchants can keep receiving payments even when other digital payment methods are not available.
This will make the digital euro more resilient and will also better protect privacy. With offline payments, details of the transaction remain exclusively between the payor and the payee, very much like cash payments today.
How exactly will we be able to use the digital euro? Will a new app be available?
There will be two options. Banks will be able to integrate the digital euro into the apps their clients already use, while the Eurosystem will offer an easy-to-use, standardised, reliable app with the basic functions.
Even if you use the latter option, your relationship will nevertheless still be with your own bank; the ECB will not open accounts for people.
But what will this European app be used for?
Just as banknotes are the same throughout the euro area, the digital euro app will also offer a common point of access. The digital euro must be accessible to everyone, regardless of their country, their age or their digital skills. We have incorporated accessibility from the design stage onwards, and have been working with organisations representing those with disabilities.
We are implementing a clear principle set out in the European Commission's legislative proposal, i.e. the choice of how to access and use the digital euro should remain in users’ hands and not be controlled by payment service providers.
Will the ECB decide how much digital euro will be issued, based on a limit set each year, just like it does for banknotes and coins?
No. As is the case for cash, it will be up to citizens and firms to determine the digital euro’s use based on demand.
On which technological platform will the digital euro run?
It will run on a common European infrastructure developed exclusively by European providers, on which banks and private operators will be able to build new services.
We’ve already seen this in our innovation programmes: more than 70 operators worked with the ECB to explore the options the digital euro offers to provide new services to their customers. Some firms have already put forward solutions, such as automatic digital receipts or automatic payment upon delivery for online purchases. These are tangible innovations that will make life easier for people and firms.
We have just launched a second call for new ideas and projects, with the aim of speeding up innovation and creating new growth opportunities for the European payments industry.
Banks have complained because they are afraid of being left out of the digital euro loop. Are their fears justified?
Dialogue with the banking sector has been, and continues to be, an essential component of the project. The digital euro has not been devised as a replacement for banks, but to integrate and strengthen their own payment services. It will in fact be the banks and other authorised intermediaries that will distribute the digital euro, manage customer relationships and develop new services. The digital euro’s common standards will enable payment solutions developed in Europe to reach customers and merchants throughout the euro area.
Is it conceivable that one day there will only be the digital euro?
I don’t think so, and I don’t think that’s what anyone is aiming for. The goal is to create a payment system in which cash, the digital euro and the services already offered by banks coexist in such a way that resilience will be guaranteed and consumers will have freedom of choice.
How can cyberattacks be prevented?
The digital euro’s security will be built on multiple layers: advanced encryption, data segregation and regular testing for simulated attacks. The infrastructure will also be distributed across several European regions to ensure continuity of service even if part of the system were to become temporarily unavailable
